No ongoing training had been provided to prison officers since initial training on basic life support or first aid, meaning that officers confronted with discovery of a ligature situation were unable to provide immediate and basic life support due to a lack of confidence and unfamiliarity of what to do in a situation when every second can count in promoting the chances of an optimal recovery
lack of immediate basic life support in ligature situations

Whilst each individual pharmacy had in-house safety checks to safeguard against over prescribing by their own pharmacy, there is no integrated system in place which would alert a prescriber to prescriptions that have been dispensed by other on-line pharmacies. As a result, it is currently possible for a patient to obtain excessive quantities of medication by simply placing multiple orders with different on-line pharmacists.

There is no requirement for the on-line pharmacies to share information with the patient's GP. This means that, in the absence of the patient's consent to share information, the online prescriber is reliant on the accuracy and truthfulness of the history provided by the patient.

Lack of information sharing also creates a risk that a GP or Pharmacist Prescriber may unwittingly prescribe a medication that is contraindicated with a medication that has been dispensed through an on-line pharmacy.

The Recovery & Discharge Plans contained inaccurate information regarding Ania's consent to share information with her mother. The evidence was that this was an entry made in error in June 2020 and was not picked up by any of the nurses who updated the Recovery & Discharge Plan over the subsequent 11 months.

The Recovery & Discharge Plans did not address the risks associated with Ania's procurement of Propranolol from on-line pharmacies. The evidence was that an update of the Recovery & Discharge Plan involved members of nursing staff simply adding a note that the overdoses had taken place. The Plan did not show that any meaningful thought had been given to addressing the particular risk associated with the procurement of on-line medication.

Mandatory refresher training on basic aspects of nursing care such as record keeping, searches, care-planning, undertaking pre- and post-leave assessments and confidentiality is not provided to staff.
discharge planning including communication with GPs and families around risk was not effective
no clear evidence of consideration of discharge medication and risk around prescribing of medication post discharge from the EDU

The purpose of the referral to South Trafford CMHT by the nurse mental health practitioner on behalf of the general practice, was for Mr Hughes to be referred to the HBTT. This was as a direct alternative to hospital admission.
delayed referral to home based treatment team

Moreover, with regard to a referral in the circumstances of this matter, the CMHT do not operate over the weekend. This meant that from Friday 20th June 2025 at 17:00, there could be no assessment and no referral to the HBTT, until 09:00 on Monday 23rd June 2025, at the earliest.
It was during this period of delay that Mr Hughes took his own life.
The After Action Review Report produced by the CMHT after Mr [name redacted] death, identified the following as a 'Concern/Gap' : 'To explore whether PCN Nurses can refer directly to HBTT.'

In evidence, it was accepted on behalf of the CMHT that there are occasions when a nurse associated with a general practice, or a general practitioner, may need to refer directly to the HBTT; but that the formal procedure does not allow for this.

Therefore, at the time of Mr [name redacted] death, such a referral could not be made. It still cannot be made, notwithstanding the availability of this course in other boroughs and the findings of the After Action Review.
